The French-inspired mansion in California’s Silicon Valley that NFL Hall of Famer Jerry Rice built for himself is back on the market, asking $35 million. The 49ers legend built the estate at 267 Atherton Ave. in the early 2000s, and it sits on 1.24 acres, according to a report by SFGATE.The 49ers legend, who won three Super Bowl titles, used this mansion as his personal residence from 2001 to 2013, according to Mansion Global. This Atherton mansion was a long-term project. It took him years to plan and build.The house, spanning 12,520 square feet, was a major undertaking. Reports from the time say it took years to plan and build, with Rice pushing for exact details throughout. “This is an incredible Atherton estate home that was built with no expense spared in the early 2000s. It was arguably one of the best and most state-of-the-art homes in Atherton at the time of its construction,” listing agent Alex Buljan of Compass told SFGATE.The interiors reflect that effort. Versace limestone floors run throughout the house, and Swarovski crystal accents add extra sparkle to the details.The Juliet balconies, Venetian plastered walls, tall ceilings and exquisite French doors and windows overlooking tranquil gardens are also some of the highlights of the breathtaking mansion."The cleverly laid out estate is hidden inside a peaceful Mediterranean garden imagined by Santana Rows landscape architect," the listing says.The home has six bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, spread across three floors connected by an elevator. The main living areas look out over the grounds, and the central kitchen is large enough for a crowd.The property also has a pool and spa, an outdoor kitchen and dining area, a stone fireplace and a putting green, all designed for entertaining guests. The property also comes with a guest house with its own kitchen.The parking is below ground. The underground garage can accommodate seven cars. Another perk of the mansion is the privacy it offers. Buljan told the outlet that the home is a ‘rare combination of location, privacy and acreage’. “It’s exceptionally private.”Another highlight of the mansion is its gym. Few sellers keep their workout equipment in the listing, but Rice did. The current listing says his gym still has his gear, along with a sauna.The mansion also comes with a theatre room. It has Art Deco touches and tiered seating. There is a wine cellar with space for 1,000 bottles, as well as a hobby room and a dog run.Meanwhile, the house has not always been easy to sell. Rice first listed the mansion in 2007 for $22 million. The sale took years to close. Earlier reports say a buyer backed out of a deal before the sale went through. Eventually, it was sold for $9 million, less than half the original asking price.After Rice sold the home in 2013, philanthropists Peter and Susanna Pau purchased it. The new $35 million asking price is a big jump from that sale, putting the house in rare company on the Peninsula. The house carries Rice’s NFL history, along with a sale price that has already surprised the market once.
Article Summary: NFL Hall of Famer Jerry Rice built the 12,520-square-foot mansion in California's Silicon Valley in the early 2000s. The home has six bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, spread across three floors connected by an elevator. The main living areas look out over the grounds, and the central kitchen is large enough for a crowd. The property also has a pool and spa, an outdoor kitchen and dining area, and a putting green.

Article Title: A 16-foot Burmese python weighing 147.9 pounds was released after radio-tagging in Florida; US scientists are now testing drones to track invasive snakes across the Everglades
Article Text:
Image: Canva

How United States scientists use drones to monitor invasive Burmese pythons across the Everglades

The 16-foot, 147.9-pound female Burmese python that was radio-tagged

Why Burmese pythons threaten Everglades mammals and why tracking them across difficult terrain is hard (Image: Canva)

How radio tracking equipment and cameras improve python detection efficiency

Why Burmese pythons threaten Everglades mammals and why tracking them across difficult terrain is hard

How drone training for Department of the Interior scientists brought python tracking to the Everglades

Why further testing matters for python control

Deep in the Florida Everglades, a vast and difficult landscape, scientists are trying a new way to find invasive Burmese pythons; they are looking from above. Researchers are testing small drones fitted with radio tracking equipment or cameras to locate snakes more efficiently, follow their movements across difficult terrain, and cut the cost of searching from the ground. One female python released after tagging measured 16 feet and weighed 147.9 pounds. In this article, you will learn how the technology works, why pythons are so hard to track, what the scientists hope to gain, and what important questions remain unanswered.The United States Geological Survey, a federal science agency, is testing a different approach to a long-running wildlife problem. Scientists at its Fort Collins Science Centre are using uncrewed aircraft systems, commonly called drones, to track invasive Burmese pythons and to learn more about how the snakes move across a vast and difficult landscape. The work is described in the center's September 2026 series, which highlights how its projects support sound decision-making. The python project stands out because the agency's own account calls it a novel use of technology that is more commonly applied to monitoring rivers and forests.A photograph published by the USGS captures the technology at work. In the image, agency biologists operate a small uncrewed aircraft system while University of Florida interns release a newly radio-tagged female Burmese python, 16 feet long and weighing 147.9 pounds, back into the Greater Everglades Ecosystem.The scene shows how the pieces fit together: a snake carrying a radio tag, people on the ground handling it safely, and an aircraft overhead testing how well the tag can be followed from the sky.The agency explains that the aircraft can carry either radio tracking equipment or a camera. The platform is being evaluated as a way to improve detection and tracking efficiency, collect better data, and reduce the labour and operating costs of traditional ground-based monitoring for pythons. In plain terms, a drone can cover wet, thick, hard-to-walk areas far faster than a person on foot, and it can pick up a tagged snake's signal or spot the animal from overhead. If it works well, fewer people would need to spend long hours searching difficult ground.The reason for all this effort is the size of the problem. The United States Geological Survey leads federal research to control the Burmese python, which has become firmly established across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem and poses a serious threat to native wildlife. The snake can grow to more than 17 feet long and is believed to be a key factor in the sharp decline of mammal populations in the region. Finding such a well-camouflaged animal in a huge, wet landscape is slow and costly, which explains why scientists are eager to test aerial tools.The idea grew out of a training program. Chris Holmquist-Johnson, a certified instructor in uncrewed aircraft systems for the Department of the Interior, trained a group of Fort Collins Science Centre scientists working in the Florida Everglades about a year before the article was published. Those researchers are now using the technology to track Burmese pythons and are gaining new insight into their movement behaviour. Holmquist-Johnson's main work involves rivers and forests in the western United States, including mapping changes in river channels and surveying thinned forest areas, so the Everglades project shows how skills built in one setting can be carried into another.It is important to read the project for what it is. The agency describes the aircraft as a tool still under evaluation, and the sources do not report measured results, such as how many more snakes are found or how much money is saved. The 16-foot, 147.9-pound snake is a single example from a photograph, not an average, and the agency notes that pythons can grow even longer. As testing continues, the key questions will be how reliably the aircraft locate tagged and untagged snakes, and whether the savings in time and cost hold up across the seasons and the many kinds of habitat in the Everglades.
Article Summary: Scientists at the US Geological Survey are using uncrewed aircraft systems to track invasive Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades. The platform is being evaluated as a way to improve detection and tracking efficiency, collect better data, and reduce the labour and operating costs of traditional ground-based monitoring. If it works well, fewer people would need to spend long hours searching difficult ground. One female python released after tagging measured 16 feet and weighed 147.9 pounds.

Article Title: Florida rebuilt a degraded offshore oyster reef with dolomite limestone in 2018; within six months live-oyster density rose from near zero to 91 per square metre, and by year five it had reached 244
Article Text:
Florida restored a degraded oyster reef in 2018; density rose to 91 per sq m in six months and 244 by year five (Image Credit: UF/IFAS)

How Florida’s oyster reef deteriorated

Why researchers chose dolomite limestone

Oyster density increased over five years

Benefits for wildlife and local oyster harvesters

What the restoration means for Florida’s coast

Florida’s Lone Cabbage Reef, once a productive oyster habitat that had deteriorated into a sandbar, began recovering after researchers and local oyster harvesters rebuilt it with dolomite limestone in 2018. According to the University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS), the restoration created a suitable surface for oyster larvae to settle and grow. A research study published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries subsequently documented the scale of that recovery, with live-oyster density at fixed restored offshore stations rising from near zero to 91 per square metre within six months and reaching 244 by the fifth year. The findings show how rebuilding lost reef structure can help revive a damaged marine ecosystem, although restoration alone cannot reverse every cause of oyster decline.Lone Cabbage Reef lies near the mouth of the East Pass of the Suwannee River in Suwannee Sound, along Florida’s Gulf Coast. Historically, it supported oyster populations, provided habitat for fish and wildlife, and helped reduce wave action along the shoreline.Over roughly three decades, however, oyster numbers declined until the once-thriving reef collapsed and became a sandbar. The loss mattered beyond the oysters themselves. Healthy oyster reefs provide habitat for other marine life, support fisheries and help protect coastal areas from waves.Researchers spent more than a decade investigating the problem and testing possible restoration methods. Field assessments and smaller experiments conducted between 2010 and 2017 suggested that the reef’s recovery was being limited by the lack of suitable hard surfaces, rather than a shortage of oyster larvae. That distinction shaped the restoration strategy: instead of relying on oysters to return to the degraded seabed on their own, the project rebuilt the physical structure they needed to settle and grow.The large-scale restoration was completed in the summer of 2018 with support from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. The project brought together University of Florida researchers, local contractors, quarry operators and members of the Cedar Key Oystermen’s Association. The team placed locally sourced dolomite limestone across the footprint of the degraded reef. Rocks measuring between six and 36 inches were used to recreate the uneven structure of a natural oyster reef. The restored surface was also built to an elevation of about 15 to 18 inches, similar to nearby healthy reefs.This design was important because oyster larvae, known as spat, need a firm surface on which to attach and grow. The gaps between rocks also provided places for young oysters to settle. The approach produced early results. According to UF/IFAS, oyster larvae appeared within a few months of construction, and monitoring showed that the restored reef’s oyster population increased annually during the five years following restoration.The research paper, Restoration is a partial but not complete solution for long-term declines in oyster populations: A case history from the northeastern Gulf of America, examined the reef’s recovery through repeated monitoring and comparisons between restored and unrestored areas. At four fixed restored offshore monitoring stations, mean live-oyster density increased from near zero to 91 oysters per square metre within six months. By the fifth year, it had reached 244 oysters per square metre.The study also examined the wider reef landscape. Across restored offshore sites and post-restoration monitoring periods, average oyster density was approximately 83 oysters per square metre. Model-based estimates for restored offshore reefs reached 218 oysters per square metre during the final sampling period. These figures describe different measurements: the 244 figure comes from fixed monitoring stations, while the 218 figure represents a model-based estimate at the broader landscape scale.Unrestored reefs did not show the same consistent recovery. Depending on their distance from shore, oyster densities at these sites either remained broadly stable or declined during the same period. The researchers concluded that restoring the underlying reef structure helped re-establish the conditions oysters needed to survive and grow. Fishing activity and river discharge also mattered to the wider ecosystem, but their associations with oyster density were weaker and less consistent once restoration was considered.The recovery had practical implications for the local fishing community. UF/IFAS reported that oyster sizes at restored and unrestored sites had become similar within three years of the work. In the portion of the restored reef open to commercial harvesting, local oyster harvesters began finding legally sized oysters on and near the reef in 2022.Estimates indicated that the work generated $5.08 million in total industry output, including $3.02 million in regional value added, and supported 44 full-time and part-time jobs with $1.01 million in labour income. However, the results do not mean that rebuilding one reef can solve Florida’s wider oyster losses. UF/IFAS estimates that the Lone Cabbage restoration replaced only about 3% to 4% of the oyster reef area lost across the Big Bend region. Monitoring also found no evidence that the restoration changed salinity patterns in Suwannee Sound, based on measurements collected at six locations over more than five years.The Lone Cabbage project demonstrates that large-scale oyster reef restoration can produce sustained improvements when the underlying habitat is rebuilt appropriately. It also highlights the value of combining scientific research with the knowledge of people who depend on the ecosystem for their livelihoods. The researchers caution, however, that restoration is only part of the solution. The causes of widespread oyster declines in the region remain incompletely understood, and the loss of reefs must be addressed on a much larger scale. The central lesson is that providing suitable limestone substrate can help oysters return to a degraded reef, but lasting recovery will also require understanding why oyster populations declined in the first place and protecting the remaining reef habitats.
Article Summary: Florida restored a degraded oyster reef in 2018. Live-oyster density rose from near zero to 91 per sq m in six months. By the fifth year, it had reached 244 oysters per square metre. Healthy oyster reefs provide habitat for other marine life, support fisheries and help protect coastal areas from waves.

Article Title: An 8-year-old Indiana boy spotted a smoking camper trailer and alerted people nearby before it caught fire; he was honoured with Department Patch and Certificate of Recognition for preventing a larger
Article Text:
A small act with a potentially big impact

Fire department recognises community spirit

Why early warnings matter

An eight-year-old boy in Indiana has received recognition from a volunteer fire department after noticing a smoking camper trailer and alerting people nearby, helping ensure firefighters were called before the situation became more serious. According to local broadcaster Eagle Country 99.3 and the Blooming Grove Volunteer Fire Department, Carter Hicks was presented with a department patch and a Certificate of Recognition for his actions. The incident occurred during the summer, when Carter noticed smoke coming from a camper trailer that appeared to be catching fire. Rather than ignore the warning signs, he informed people in the vicinity, prompting a fire department response. The department later honoured Carter for his awareness and initiative, highlighting how his concern for another person’s property helped bring attention to a potentially dangerous situation.For firefighters, recognising the early signs of an emergency can make a significant difference. Smoke coming from a trailer can indicate a developing fire, and drawing attention to it quickly gives people an opportunity to respond before the situation escalates.In Carter’s case, his decision to alert those nearby helped ensure the problem was noticed and brought to the attention of emergency responders. The department’s recognition focused not only on his quick thinking but also on his concern for the safety and property of others. His actions demonstrated how remaining alert and responding responsibly can make a meaningful difference during potentially dangerous situations. Details about the cause of the smoke, the extent of any damage and whether anyone was injured were not included in the initial local news report.Members of the Blooming Grove Volunteer Fire Department presented Carter with the patch and certificate during a recognition ceremony held on the Saturday before the October 8 report. The department praised the youngster’s sense of responsibility, noting that community members can play an important role in identifying hazards and alerting others, even without formal emergency training.The recognition also carried a broader message about public service: making a difference does not always require specialised equipment or an official role. Paying attention to one’s surroundings and speaking up when something appears unsafe can be valuable contributions to community safety.Fire safety guidance consistently stresses the importance of treating smoke and other possible signs of fire seriously. The US Fire Administration advises people to get to safety and contact emergency services when they encounter a fire, rather than putting themselves at risk by attempting to tackle it.Carter’s response offered a simple example of that principle. He noticed something unusual, alerted other people and helped bring the situation to the attention of firefighters.At eight years old, he was not expected to fight the fire himself. His contribution came from recognising that something was wrong and making sure others knew about it. His actions also highlight the importance of teaching children to stay calm, recognise potential hazards and seek help from trusted adults or emergency services when dangerous situations arise. The department’s decision to honour him underscores how awareness, responsibility and consideration for others can matter in an emergency, regardless of age.
Article Summary: Carter Hicks noticed smoke coming from a camper trailer that appeared to be catching fire. Rather than ignore the warning signs, he informed people in the vicinity, prompting a fire department response. Blooming Grove Volunteer Fire Department presented Carter with a department patch and a Certificate of Recognition.

Article Title: A Massachusetts dairy farmer nearly sold an unfarmable slice of his land to Walmart, but put an 11-acre solar field there instead; the lease paid $1,000 a week while rooftop panels erased a $1,400 mon
Article Text:
Representative image

A difficult piece of farmland

The value of solar on the barn

Representative image

Leasing land to harvest sunshine

A different kind of farm income

Keeping the land in the family

A Massachusetts dairy farmer once considered selling an awkward, hard-to-farm patch of his property to Walmart. Instead, he turned the 11-acre slice into a solar field that now provides a steady lease income, while rooftop panels have nearly wiped out the farm’s $1,400 monthly electricity bill. The story was told by John Nagy in Notre Dame Magazine in 'The Sun Farmers', a feature also republished by the Let’s Share the Sun Foundation. It follows George Hunt Jr., whose decision to combine farming with solar power created a new source of income without giving up the land. His experience shows how a property that seemed unsuitable for crops could still contribute to the farm, the local energy supply and the family’s long-term plans. Read on to know more about it here:Hunt’s farm was a working dairy operation, with hundreds of acres and a herd of about 250 cows. Like many dairy farmers, he had to balance the costs of running the farm against the uncertain returns from milk. He also wanted to leave his children a business that could support a decent quality of life without requiring them to milk an enormous herd every day.One part of the property presented a different kind of challenge. The 11-acre plot was levelled land that was difficult to farm. According to Nagy’s account, Hunt considered selling it to Walmart, which was interested in the site.The retailer’s offer could have turned the unproductive parcel into a straightforward financial gain.But Hunt began to see another possibility. Solar panels could make use of land that was not well suited to growing crops, while allowing the farm to retain ownership. Rather than sell the site outright, he could lease it to a solar developer and earn regular income from the land.The decision did not happen in isolation. Massachusetts had created incentives for solar power, including renewable energy credits, and the state’s solar programme had targets that encouraged development. Those policies helped make solar a viable option for farmers and other landowners.Before committing to a larger project, Hunt had already installed solar panels on the roof of his barn. The array supplied power for many of the farm’s daily needs, including pumping water, cooling milk, operating milking equipment and running lights.When writer Nagy visited in 2015, he shared in his article that Hunt said the rooftop system had almost eliminated the farm’s monthly electricity bill of about $1,400. It also generated a small refund during much of the year for electricity sent back to the grid. For a dairy farm with substantial energy needs, reducing a major monthly expense offered a practical benefit beyond the environmental appeal of renewable power.The rooftop system gave Hunt confidence to consider a much larger solar project. If panels could help manage the farm’s own electricity costs, a ground-mounted array could make productive use of the land that had little value for conventional farming.Hunt’s experience also highlights the importance of careful advice when navigating a complicated industry. The feature describes solar consultant Bill Jordan reviewing an earlier contract and helping Hunt identify a federal grant that had been overlooked. Hunt offered to pay Jordan for the work, but Jordan returned the check after the original contractor said it would prepare the grant application.Hunt eventually chose solar over selling the awkward parcel to Walmart. The 11-acre site became part of a 3-megawatt solar array that supplied electricity to the city of Lowell, Massachusetts, according to Nagy’s report.The arrangement gave Hunt a land-lease payment of $1,000 a week. While the income was reportedly less than the amount Walmart had offered to buy the land, it provided a recurring return while Hunt kept ownership of the property. The farmer described himself as pleased with the decision and came to see himself as a “sun farmer,” as per the report.That phrase captures the unusual way the project fit into the farm. Hunt continued to raise cows, produce milk and manage the agricultural business, but the leased land created another kind of harvest. Instead of crops, the field produced electricity, while the lease payment supported the farm’s finances.Solar also created opportunities beyond the main array. Hunt was considering additional panels for other buildings on the property, including a structure used as an indoor sports arena. The electricity could serve tenants at a nearby restaurant and help reduce their energy costs.The solar lease was particularly valuable because dairy income could fluctuate. As per the report, Hunt told Nagy that farmers might receive a good price for milk only every few years, making it important to find other sources of revenue. His farm already diversified through activities such as selling firewood and hay and investing in local real estate.The solar project added another layer to that approach. It did not replace dairy farming, but gave Hunt a reliable income stream from land that was difficult to use for crops. The rooftop panels, meanwhile, reduced the farm’s operating expenses by addressing one of its largest utility costs.That combination matters. A lease payment can help with income, but avoiding a recurring electricity bill can be just as useful to a business that operates equipment every day. The systems addressed two separate financial pressures: one through revenue from the leased field and the other through lower power costs.Hunt also helped connect other farmers with Jordan, passing along the names of 25 or 30 people interested in solar. The feature notes that successful referrals brought him a small commission. His experience had become a practical example for other landowners weighing whether solar could fit their operations.For Hunt, the choice was not simply between Walmart and solar panels. It was about how to make a difficult piece of land work for the farm’s future. Selling would have provided an immediate payment, but leasing the land created recurring income and allowed the family to retain ownership.The rooftop installation also helped make the wider farm more financially resilient. By reducing an electricity bill of about $1,400 a month to almost nothing, the system freed up money that would otherwise have gone to power costs. The 11-acre field added a separate weekly lease payment, giving the farm a second benefit from solar.Hunt’s story offers a grounded example of how renewable energy can fit into an existing business. It did not require him to stop farming or convert the whole property. Instead, the panels occupied land that was hard to farm and helped power homes, businesses and municipal operations elsewhere.A patch of land once considered for a big-box store became part of a local energy project. Hunt kept his farm, gained a weekly lease payment and cut a major monthly expense. In a business where margins can be tight and conditions change from year to year, the sun became another crop worth cultivating.
Article Summary: George Hunt Jr. considered selling an awkward, hard-to-farm patch of his property to Walmart. Instead, he turned the 11-acre slice into a solar field that now provides a steady lease income. rooftop panels have nearly wiped out the farm’s $1,400 monthly electricity bill.

Article Title: 15 guanacos were taken to a remote Falklands island in the 1930s; their descendants kept their genetic diversity through two severe population crashes
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why John Hamilton shipped fifteen guanacos to Staats Island in the late 1930s

Guanaco sharing a habitat with Magellanic penguins, Punta Tombo (Image: Wikipedia)

How a cull in the late 1950s cut the Staats Island guanaco herd from 300 animals

What scientists measured in guanacos from eight localities

Guanacos near the La Silla Observatory, 2400 meters above sea level (Image: Wikipedia)

Staats Island guanacos match most mainland herds

Genetic evidence points to Monte León in southern Patagonia

Fast regrowth helped the island herd keep its genetic variety

What the guanaco findings mean for conservation

In the late 1930s, a small group of guanacos, native South American camelids, was shipped from southern Patagonia to Staats Island, a remote, treeless Falklands island. Only fifteen animals founded the entire herd. Roughly twenty-five years later, a cull reduced it from about 300 animals to between 10 and 20. Such a herd would be expected to lose much of its genetic variety. Yet scientists who studied the herd more than six decades after its founding found something truly surprising. Their analysis showed the island herd still holds genetic diversity comparable to most mainland populations, despite two severe population crashes.According to a 2014 study, ‘ Maintenance of Genetic Diversity in an Introduced Island Population of Guanacos after Seven Decades and Two Severe Demographic Bottlenecks: Implications for Camelid Conservation ’ by Benito González, Pablo Orozco-terWengel, Rainer von Borries, Warren Johnson, William Franklin and Juan Marín in the journal PLOS One, guanacos were brought to the Falkland Islands, also known as Islas Malvinas, in the late 1930s by John Hamilton. He introduced them, together with several other Patagonian species, in an attempt to diversify the local economy.The researchers explain that young animals were plausibly captured near Rio Gallegos in Argentina or Pali-Aike in Chile, then shipped to the islands.Eleven went to Sedge Island and fifteen to Staats Island. Only the Staats Island animals survived. The island covers about 500 hectares at the far western edge of an archipelago of 750 islands, roughly 600 kilometres from the South American coast, and its guanacos have stayed isolated from other populations for more than seventy years.The herd prospered at first. According to the study, attempts were later made to eradicate it, to reduce overgrazing and convert the island to sheep farming. This severe culling in the late 1950s drove the population down from 300 animals to its smallest size, between 10 and 20 individuals, in the early 1960s.The animals were then allowed to recover, with only sporadic, low levels of poaching and culling. By 2004, the herd numbered about 400. The researchers therefore described a population that had passed through two severe bottlenecks, the founding event and the cull, each time falling below 20 animals. They expected low genetic diversity as a result.To test that expectation, the authors compared the island herd with guanacos from the adjacent mainland and from Tierra del Fuego, using samples from eight localities. They studied two kinds of genetic information, variation in the mitochondrial genetic material and variation at microsatellite markers in the nuclear genetic material. Six research expeditions visited Staats Island between 1999 and 2008, and the island samples were collected in 2004 and 2005. They came from faeces and carcasses, so no animals had to be captured or handled there.The authors also ran computer simulations of the herd's history, using a simulated mainland population of 10,000 animals that was reduced to fifteen. They compared the real genetic results with those simulations.The results contradicted the expectation. The researchers report that the genetic variation on Staats Island was comparable to most mainland populations and greater than that on Tierra del Fuego. For the mitochondrial genetic material, the island herd's haplotype diversity was 0.61, against 0.36 on Tierra del Fuego. The study notes that Tierra del Fuego holds a large population of more than 80,000 guanacos.The expected differences in the nuclear markers were not statistically significant between the island herd and the mainland as a whole. The authors explain the contrast with Tierra del Fuego by history. That island's guanacos were isolated thousands of years ago, roughly 8,000 years before the study, so drift has had far longer to act, whereas the Staats Island herd has existed for only about 65 years. The mitochondrial markers did show that the island herd had drifted further from the mainland populations than the mainland populations differ from one another.The study also asked where the founders came from. Of the 23 mitochondrial haplotypes found across all samples, the Staats Island herd carried only three. All three were shared with the Monte León population on the coast of southern Patagonia, the only mainland population that held all of them together. The island's most common haplotype appeared on the mainland only at Monte León.Assignment tests supported this. The authors report that 19 of the 20 Staats Island animals tested grouped with the southern Patagonian cluster. Monte León lies about 150 kilometres north of Rio Gallegos, the port the animals were shipped from. The guanaco population that once lived near Rio Gallegos has since disappeared locally or moved elsewhere. The authors conclude that most of the island's genetic background came from Monte León or a similar population, while some variation may have come from neighbouring southern populations, which matches the historical records.The authors suggest the most likely explanation is that the fifteen founders were a random sample of a mainland population that was already genetically diverse. They add that both population crashes lasted only a few generations and were followed by rapid growth, which can wipe out much of the genetic trace a bottleneck leaves behind.Their simulation showed the effect on different measures. The first bottleneck cut the average number of gene variants per marker by about 29 per cent, from 12.8 to 9.1, while expected heterozygosity, another measure of diversity, fell by only 3.5 per cent. The second bottleneck reduced the number of variants to roughly 51 per cent of the original, without affecting expected heterozygosity. One statistical test did detect signs of a past bottleneck on Staats Island, but the authors say their analyses did not find a consistent bottleneck signal overall.The authors call the result surprising and say it offers hope for small, surviving remnant populations on the mainland, which could be holding on to genetic diversity despite low numbers. They stress, however, that this does not mean severe culling or hunting would leave a population's fitness untouched. They add that guanacos on Staats Island are currently suffering neonatal malformations and mortality, and they warn against letting either the island or the Patagonian populations fall to severely low numbers.The study also points to the pressure on mainland guanacos. They were hunted to free up land for sheep and for their pelts. Chile exported about 35,000 pelts during the twentieth century, and Argentina exported 223,000 in only four years, from 1976 to 1979. The authors note that guanaco wool is worth 60 to 80 United States dollars per kilogram, that the Staats Island guanacos are privately owned, and that their future is unknown. They call for genetic assessments of critically small and isolated guanaco populations across the species' range.
Article Summary: A small group of guanacos was shipped from southern Patagonia to Staats Island in the late 1930s. Only fifteen animals founded the entire herd. Roughly twenty- five years later, a cull reduced it from about 300 animals to between 10 and 20. Such a herd would be expected to lose much of its genetic variety. Yet scientists who studied the herd more than six decades after its founding found something truly surprising. Their analysis showed the island herd still holds genetic diversity comparable to most mainland populations.

Article Title: An Arkansas family treated the same fence as its property line for nearly six decades; after new neighbours removed fencing and trees, an appeals court upheld $12,000 in treble damages and an order to
Article Text:
The fence became more than just a fence

Tree removal resulted in $12,000 damages

The fence must be rebuilt

A fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties, after a dispute over trees and fencing reached the state Court of Appeals. The ruling in Floyd v. Bowlin-Lemon, reported by Justia, Leagle and Case Law Wire, affirmed the Bowlins’ boundary claim, a $12,000 treble-damages award and an order requiring the neighbouring owners to rebuild the fence. The case involved adjoining properties in Crawford County and centred on a fence line that the Bowlin family had treated as its southern boundary for decades. According to the Arkansas Court of Appeals, Joy Bowlin-Lemon’s family acquired the property in 1967. The family was shown the existing fence lines when it purchased the land and subsequently used those fences as practical boundaries. The property was used for livestock, including cattle and horses, while the family also maintained the land up to the fence by brush hogging and cutting hay.That arrangement remained unchallenged for decades. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property.The court record says portions of the longstanding fence were removed beginning in 2017, with the fence eventually torn down. Trees in the disputed area were also cut down. The Bowlins eventually filed a lawsuit in 2023, alleging trespass and destruction of their fencing and trees. A Crawford County Circuit Court trial followed in October 2024.The central legal question was whether years of treating the fence as the boundary could establish a legally recognised boundary even if the fence did not precisely match the surveyed property line. The appeals court said yes.Under Arkansas law, a boundary by acquiescence can arise when neighbouring landowners tacitly accept a particular line as the dividing boundary for a long period. The court noted that an express agreement is not required, nor does there need to have been an earlier dispute over the property line.In this case, the decades of maintenance and use along the fence, combined with the absence of objections from neighbouring owners, provided sufficient evidence for the lower court’s decision. The court also noted that the southern fence extended roughly 30 to 40 feet beyond the surveyed property line. Despite that discrepancy, the long-established conduct surrounding the fence supported its recognition as the boundary.The dispute also became costly for the Floyds. The circuit court determined that the trees removed from the disputed area were worth $4,000. The Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld that valuation, finding that testimony about the number and type of trees, photographs of the property and evidence of the clearing provided enough support.The court also upheld treble damages, bringing the total award to $12,000. Arkansas law allows treble damages when someone cuts, destroys or removes trees belonging to another person. The appeals court found enough evidence to support the finding that the tree removal was intentional or, at minimum, sufficiently reckless or negligent to trigger the statute. Among the evidence considered was the presence of no-trespassing signs along the fence and Ty Floyd’s admission that he removed trees and portions of the fencing.The lower court also ordered the Floyds to rebuild fencing along the eastern and southern boundaries. The appeals court left that order intact. It noted that Ty Floyd had indicated during the trial that he was willing to rebuild the fence, while his attorney did not object when the Bowlins requested the injunction.That meant the Floyds could not later challenge the fence-rebuilding requirement on appeal. There was, however, one issue the appeals court sent back to the circuit court. The original judgment did not contain a sufficiently precise legal description of the boundary. The appeals court therefore remanded the case for the limited purpose of adding a specific description that would allow the established boundary to be identified directly from the judgment.The decision underscores how decades of conduct can matter in property disputes. A fence may begin as a practical marker, but when generations of adjoining owners consistently treat it as the dividing line, that conduct can ultimately carry legal weight, even when a later survey points somewhere else.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments box below.
Article Summary: Fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property. The Bowlin family had treated the fence line as its southern boundary for decades.

Article Title: ‘The Orange Plague’: Why a golden, naked Trump is sitting on another man
Article Text:
File photo: Visitors looks at a scupture titled "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiot

What does the statue symbolise?

Why is Trump depicted naked?

Why has the statue been installed at the European Parliament?

Where else has ‘The Orange Plague’ been displayed?

A 2.6-metre-tall statue of US president Donald Trump, naked and coated in 23-karat gold leaf, has been installed inside the European parliament in Strasbourg, France.Titled ‘The Orange Plague’, the sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man’s head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the “King of Injustice”.The sculpture is a satirical critique of what Galschiøt sees as Trump’s threats to the environment, international cooperation and the rules-based world order. The artist has said the US president is destroying the causes and institutions he believes in, including efforts to tackle climate change. The work also questions how political power is exercised and how its consequences are borne by those with less power.The smaller man beneath Trump represents the burden imposed by the powerful on the less powerful.A plaque at the base of the sculpture captures the imbalance through the words: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except step down from his back.”The imagery suggests a leader who claims to help others while continuing to place the weight of his power and decisions on them.The golf club and scales of justice add to the political satire, juxtaposing Trump’s personal image with the idea of justice. Its gold finish is also a deliberate choice: Galschiøt has pointed to Trump’s fondness for gold, saying he believes the president might even like the sculpture.Galschiøt has said the sculpture draws inspiration from Danish author Hans Christian Andersen’s fairy tale ‘The Emperor’s New Clothes’, in which a vain emperor parades through his city naked while those around him pretend he is wearing magnificent clothes.This is also not the first Trump sculpture to depict Trump naked based on a correlation with the fairy tale, a previous series of statues displayed across the US by an artist collective was also titled, ‘The Emperor Has No Balls’.By depicting Trump naked, Galschiøt seeks to ridicule the president and strip away the image of authority surrounding him. “Dictators don’t like you laughing at them,” the artist said, explaining the thinking behind the work.Galschiøt is known for provocative political art. His best-known works include the Pillar of Shame, a memorial to victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre that was controversially removed from a Hong Kong university in 2021. He has drawn a parallel between the two works, saying both concern the relationship between the powerful and the powerless.The exhibition was sponsored by Danish politician Per Clausen, a member of the European parliament’s left-wing group, The Left. Members of the European Parliament are entitled to sponsor cultural events and exhibitions on parliamentary premises, subject to approval by officials. The sculpture’s installation therefore does not amount to an official endorsement of its message by the European Union.Clausen said he wanted to encourage debate about how power is used around the world and how Europe can protect its interests without becoming dependent on Trump. He defended the exhibition as an opportunity to display work that not everyone might agree with.Galschiøt, who had feared the application would be rejected, viewed the approval as an opportunity to bring criticism of Trump into the European Parliament. He said many Europeans regard the US president’s conduct as a serious problem, even if they recognise that he is the leader of an important ally.The sculpture has previously been displayed at the Munich Security Conference and the COP30 United Nations climate conference in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025. It was also shown at demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier in 2026 calling for Greenland to be protected from US ambitions.The Strasbourg installation was accompanied by 3D-printed miniature versions of the sculpture, distributed to visitors as “protest tokens”. The artist has said he produced around 20,000 miniatures for distribution to visitors and European Parliament staff.The temporary exhibition in Strasbourg is expected to remain on display until Thursday. Galschiøt plans to exhibit the sculpture again at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, next month. Trump has not publicly commented on the artwork.
Article Summary: Sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man's head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the ‘King of Injustice’

Article Title: US suspends 8 tech firms from PERM process: Full list and what it means
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump.

The US administration has suspended eight major technology companies from the employment-based green card process, leaving thousands of foreign professionals, including Indian IT workers, facing uncertainty over their permanent residency plans.The companies named in the October 8 order are Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.The administration has cited alleged abuse of employment-based immigration programmes and the need to protect American workers. US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off American workers while seeking H-1B approvals and green cards for foreign employees. Cognizant had also faced a suspension of its US green card filings in September amid a probe into possible visa fraud.PERM is a key step in obtaining many employer-sponsored green cards. It requires employers to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available American workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.The suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards. However, employees with pending PERM applications could face delays, while those whose employers have not yet filed applications may be unable to begin the usual process through these companies. Workers whose PERM certifications have already been approved are in a different position, as the order does not automatically invalidate existing approvals.The decision could create additional uncertainty for H-1B workers approaching the standard six-year limit, particularly those relying on their green card process to qualify for extensions. Some employees may explore sponsorship through another employer, but applications do not automatically transfer when workers change jobs.The duration of the suspension remains uncertain. JD Vance said it would continue “as long as it needs to”. The affected companies could also challenge the decision in federal court. The impact on individual workers will depend on the status of their immigration cases and the length of the suspension.
Article Summary: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini named. US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.

Article Title: A 21-year-old Tennessee moviegoer noticed an 80-year-old AMC usher emptying trash after a screening and hoped a TikTok fundraiser might bring in $500; strangers donated more than $146,000 in less than
Article Text:
Brooklyn Green spotted an elderly worker emptying rubbish at an AMC theatre in Tennessee and recorded a video of her.

Mary, the 80-year-old cinema worker

Mixed reactions to fundraiser

Mary reacts to fundraiser

A 21-year-old woman in Tennessee, United States raised more than $146,000 in less than 24 hours for an 80-year-old cinema worker after noticing her cleaning up rubbish at an AMC theatre. What began as a TikTok video and a small fundraising effort soon attracted thousands of people online, with donations far exceeding the $500 the young woman had initially hoped to collect.According to WVLT, Brooklyn Green had gone to watch a film with her grandparents at the AMC theatre in Maryville, Tennessee, when she noticed an elderly employee pushing a cleaning cart and emptying rubbish. The woman was working hard, and Green decided to record a short video of her.“I just saw her work ethic. She was just working really hard,” Green told WVLT. She later posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement.Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day. The total eventually reached approximately $146,000 before Green returned to the theatre to surprise the woman.After launching the fundraiser, Green returned to the theatre to find the elderly employee. However, the woman was not working that day. Green spoke to a manager and learnt that her name was Mary.According to the report, Mary had worked in theatres for more than 45 years. Managers told Green that she enjoyed her job and did not want to stop working. They said Mary was concerned that things might go downhill for her if she stopped working at her age.Green also learnt that Mary regularly helped other people. According to the information shared with her, Mary supported her church and people experiencing homelessness.Her willingness to help others became another reason Green wanted the fundraising effort to succeed. Green recalled a conversation with Mary about the people she supported.“She told me that she helps a mother and child and some of the homeless, and I told her that it comes back tenfold,” Green said.As the TikTok video gained attention, Green began sharing updates about the fundraising campaign. In one update, she explained that Mary was unaware of the video and the money being collected for her.Green also told followers that Mary might not want to accept the donations. According to the manager, Mary was reluctant to stop working, and Green acknowledged that the elderly woman might choose to give the money to other people or charities.The possibility prompted criticism from some social media users. They questioned whether the donations should be returned if Mary did not want the money or decided against retirement.Green responded by making it clear that Mary would have complete control over the funds. "Guys, I said she will decide regardless what to do with the donations. If she decides to give it to a charity or whatever then that is her decision. She is getting every penny, deep breaths lol," Green wrote.She also acknowledged that some people had criticised her for starting the campaign without first speaking to Mary about retirement. "I have gotten a lot of support, but also a lot of backlash for assuming she wants to retire, as well as her not being aware that I was doing this," Green told Storyful, according to CBS News.Despite the criticism, Green continued with her plan to meet Mary and personally tell her about the donations. Green eventually returned to the AMC theatre while Mary was working and surprised her with news of the fundraising campaign.By then, donations had reached approximately $146,000. Green showed Mary the amount on a tablet, revealing how much money strangers had contributed after watching the TikTok video.Mary was overwhelmed by the response and thanked everyone who had donated.“Thank you so very much to all the wonderful people that have donated money. I’m overwhelmed and certainly blessed by the Lord and you wonderful people,” Mary told WVLT.Following the surprise, Mary asked for the GoFundMe campaign to be paused. She said she had already received more than she could ask for. Meanwhile, Green has decided she will work on other projects intended to support more people.
Article Summary: Brooklyn Green, 21, recorded a video of an elderly worker at an AMC theatre in Tennessee. She posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement. Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day.

Article Title: A $132,000 GoFundMe was raised for radio host Ronn Owens; federal review found thousands spent on mortgages, businesses and family transfers
Article Text:
Longtime Bay Area radio legend Ronn Owens. Image Credit: The Mercury News

What happened to the $132,000 Ronn Owens GoFundMe donations

Ronn Owens at the KGO studio. Image Credit: The Jewish News of Northern Carolina

The federal review found most spending went elsewhere

Image Credit: SFist

Why did the bankruptcy case become part of the dispute

The court also examined family transfers and other expenses

What did the judge decide about the bankruptcy

The fundraising questions remain separate from criminal charges

A $132,000 GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses, while much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.The GoFundMe campaign was launched in January 2025 as Owens faced serious health problems. The longtime KGO radio host had described living with Parkinson’s disease for 23 years, along with four bouts of cancer, including colon cancer, and serious heart issues. The campaign appealed to people familiar with his long broadcasting career and said donations would help Owens and his family through difficult circumstances.According to TheDesk, GoFundMe ultimately paid Owens and his wife, Elizabeth Naylor, $132,480 from the campaign. The US Trustee Program in Phoenix later reviewed more than 18 months of financial records, including the bank account into which the donations were deposited.The examination found that the money was largely spent on expenses unrelated to medical care.The figures examined by the trustee provide the clearest picture of how the money was used. TheDesk reported that around $17,000 went towards medical-related bills, although it was not clear whether all of those expenses were connected specifically to Owens’ cancer treatment. By contrast, $118,898 was identified as spending unrelated to medical needs.More than $61,600 went towards mortgage payments, while nearly $44,400 was recorded as capital contributions to companies owned by Owens. The remaining spending included travel, subscriptions and cash given to a child. SFist also reported that other money went towards credit card bills and transfers to family members.The amounts were significant because the campaign had been presented against the backdrop of Owens’ worsening health and financial difficulties. The trustee’s review looked beyond the original fundraising appeal and followed the money through the couple’s accounts.The GoFundMe spending came under scrutiny during Owens and Naylor’s bankruptcy proceedings. The couple first sought Chapter 13 bankruptcy protection, but later filed under Chapter 11 after the earlier case did not provide the protection they sought. Their bankruptcy proceedings eventually brought their financial records under closer examination.SFist reported that during the period covered by the review, the family had more than $20,000 in monthly income and spent more than $520,000 from its bank accounts. The trustee found that only a relatively small portion of the couple’s financial burden was connected to medical expenses.The US Trustee then argued that the bankruptcy case should be dismissed. TheDesk reported that the trustee’s attorney pointed to the bank and GoFundMe records when assessing the couple’s ability to meet Chapter 11 requirements. The court ultimately agreed that there was no reasonable likelihood of a successful reorganisation.Another part of the financial review concerned money transferred to Owens’ daughter, Laura Owens. RadarOnline reported that financial records showed $19,608 in gifts to her, despite the couple having stated under oath that they had not made gifts worth more than $600 per person during the relevant period.The records also showed spending on consumer credit cards, retail and online purchases and other non-medical expenses. RadarOnline noted that the government did not bring criminal or civil fraud charges against Owens or Naylor, and they were not formally accused of fraud in court.The family transfers received additional attention because Laura Owens had her own legal and financial troubles. RadarOnline reported that she had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which was later dismissed, while SFist described her as financially dependent on her parents. Those circumstances formed part of the wider financial background examined during the bankruptcy proceedings.The federal bankruptcy court ultimately dismissed Owens and Naylor’s case and prevented them from filing another bankruptcy action for at least two years. TheDesk reported that Chief US Bankruptcy Judge Madeleine Wanslee cited significant failures to meet Chapter 11 requirements, along with multiple errors and misstatements in the record.The judge also pointed to changes in sworn statements concerning ownership of the home where the couple lived. Naylor agreed to the two-year restriction but disputed the suggestion that the documents and testimony demonstrated wrongdoing. According to TheDesk, she said she was grateful for the donations and had worked with the court in the interest of transparency.The ruling did not determine that the GoFundMe spending itself amounted to criminal wrongdoing. Instead, the judge allowed donors to pursue possible claims against Owens and Naylor in state court. Creditors were also allowed to resume collection efforts.The federal trustee said the financial records raised a serious question about whether GoFundMe donors received what they believed they were supporting. SFist reported that the trustee did not conclude that a law had been broken. The issue of whether the fundraising appeal and subsequent spending created legal claims was left for donors and GoFundMe to pursue outside the bankruptcy case.The campaign itself remained online at the time of SFist’s August 3 report and had raised about $137,000 against a $140,000 goal.
Article Summary: A GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses. Much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.

Article Title: Viola Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island; now she and husband Julius Tennon are donating $1.2 million to help local families
Article Text:
PC: Rhode Island Monthly

A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother

From a childhood in poverty to giving back to her Rhode Island roots

What families will be able to access at the new centre

How the new centre will support thousands of Rhode Island residents

For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood. The award-winning actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a $1.2 million investment in Central Falls, the Rhode Island community where Davis once lived. The money will fund a new family engagement centre named after her mother, Mary Alice Davis, whose influence Davis has spoken about in explaining the project. Planned as a permanent base for local services, the centre will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work.For Davis, naming the facility after her mother gives the project a personal connection. She has described the decision as a way of honouring a woman who continued to believe in people through difficult circumstances. The centre, she said, would carry that spirit forward by supporting individuals and creating opportunities for families.As reported by WJAR, the $1.2 million investment was announced on Monday, 20 July 2026. Rather than funding a single short-term initiative, the donation is intended to establish a lasting community resource in Central Falls, a city closely connected to Davis’s childhood.Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island, an experience that forms an important part of her personal history. She went on to build a career in film, television and theatre, becoming one of the most widely recognised actors of her generation. Her professional achievements have included major industry awards, but her latest investment focuses on a community far removed from the entertainment business.Central Falls was part of the environment in which Davis spent her early years. The new centre offers a way for her and Tennon to direct resources towards residents who may face financial pressures and limited access to services.The couple's contribution is being made through their foundation, which has an existing connection to Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry already serves about 3,000 people each month. The new facility is expected to provide a broader base for that work, alongside services aimed at parents, adults seeking new skills and families looking for guidance.Tennon, who is originally from Austin, Texas, has also expressed his commitment to supporting Rhode Island. Although the state is not his birthplace, he and Davis are directing the investment towards a community that holds particular significance for his wife.The planned facility will bring several services together in one location. These include a parent resource centre, a parent university and adult empowerment programmes, giving parents and other residents access to information and opportunities for learning.Food assistance will remain part of the work. The expanded Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry is expected to build on a service that already reaches thousands of people monthly. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities, educational workshops and community events.For people looking for help with more than one issue, having these services in the same place could make it easier to find the right support. Someone visiting for food assistance, for example, may also be able to access parenting resources or information about employment training.The facility will also serve as the permanent administrative headquarters of the Davis-Tennon Foundation. This gives the organisation a local base from which to coordinate its activities and maintain its work in the area.Angelo Garcia, chair of the foundation, said, "Whether someone comes seeking food, parenting resources, educational support, workforce training, or guidance through a difficult season, our goal is simple: one place where people are welcomed, connected, and empowered.”The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry provides an established starting point for the project. Its reported monthly reach of around 3,000 individuals gives an indication of the demand for food assistance in the community and the role the new centre could play in extending that support.The planned expansion will place the pantry within a wider network of family and adult services. Residents will have access not only to food assistance but also to programmes intended to support education, financial understanding and employment prospects.The centre's effectiveness will depend on how these services are delivered and how well they meet local needs once the facility is operating. The announcement sets out the intended range of programmes, although it does not specify an opening date or provide a detailed timetable for their introduction.
Article Summary: The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities.

Article Title: In 1951, a Texas town of 400 residents avoided condemnation for a federal dam; 75 years later, a 90-year-old landowner and his neighbors have temporarily halted a 30-foot border wall on the same river
Article Text:
Wall contractors in San Ygnacio, Texas (PC: Elsa Hull)

A small town with a rich history

What state records say

Joel Ruiz in San Ygnacio, Texas (PC: Elsa Hull)

Why residents are opposing the border wall

A fight over the river, too

Sheriff’s deputy confronts Elsa Hull in a bird sanctuary (PC: Maxine Rebeles)

The 1951 petition returns to the spotlight

Frank ‘Chip’ Briscoe with his son (PC: Elsa Hull)

Can the town win again?

Currently, there’s a battle going on in a small Texas town along the US-Mexico border. Now this particular land battle has also brought a forgotten chapter of history back to life. In 1951, residents of San Ygnacio successfully persuaded the US government to spare their community from condemnation for a federal dam project. But nearly 75 years later, the town is once again resisting a major government development; this time a proposed border wall that residents fear could damage their properties and harm the river ecosystem.At the centre of the latest struggle is Joel Ruiz, a 90-year-old landowner who has spent decades living beside the Rio Grande. He also runs a small fishing business. As per reports, Ruiz, along with other residents have managed to temporarily put a break on construction after confronting contractors, examining historical property records and pursuing legal action.However, this pause is not backed by a court order.San Ygnacio might be a small town but it comes with a remarkable history. Founded in 1830, it is among the oldest communities in Zapata County, southern Texas.Situated along the Rio Grande, across from Mexico, the town is known for its historic sandstone houses, traditional architecture and long connection with the border region.The Texas State Historical Association records that San Ygnacio was once a centre of trade and retains a distinctive collection of 19th-century sandstone buildings. Its historic district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.According to the Texas State Historical Association, in the early 1950s, plans for the Falcon Dam and its reservoir threatened to submerge settlements along the river. San Ygnacio was also among them.In April 1951, hundreds of residents petitioned the government to exclude their land from condemnation proceedings. Their argument was that the town stood high enough above the reservoir's projected maximum water level to remain safe from flooding. The petition succeeded, and San Ygnacio was spared from the planned acquisition.The victory became an important part of the town's history. Now, residents are drawing on those same records and challenging another federal project.The latest dispute concerns the US government's renewed border-wall expansion under President Donald Trump. The programme includes steel barriers and supporting border-security infrastructure intended to strengthen control along the US-Mexico border.In San Ygnacio, construction activity has raised questions about whether the government and its contractors have the necessary rights to work on this particular land as it is privately owned.The heavy machinery cleared vegetation and damaged parts of Ruiz's riverfront property. Residents also reported that construction affected trees and an irrigation line, while a steel barrier obstructed access to his boat ramp. The fishing business he had operated for years was also disrupted.The disagreement centres on land ownership. Federal authorities have maintained that construction is taking place on government-controlled land, while residents point to property records that they say establish their ownership of the disputed areas.Texas Public Radio reported in June 2026 that landowners questioned why clearing work had begun before they had signed right-of-entry agreements or the government had completed condemnation proceedings.For San Ygnacio's residents, the concern extends to the river. The Rio Grande is the town's sole source of drinking water, making the riverfront's future particularly important for those living there. Also, the proposed construction has also affected the area around the San Ygnacio Bird and Butterfly Sanctuary.Ruiz helped establish the sanctuary in 1973, and residents fear that the loss of vegetation and changes to the riverfront could damage the habitat they have spent decades protecting.As per reports, the Department of Homeland Security waived several federal environmental laws to accelerate border infrastructure construction. Residents and environmental advocates argue that proceeding without the usual safeguards could have lasting consequences for the river and surrounding land.Architectural conservator Frank “Chip” Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda examined property records linked to the earlier Falcon Dam dispute and found no evidence that the government had subsequently acquired the land excluded from the original condemnation.De Anda filed lawsuits alleging that the government had taken private property in violation of the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution. Following discussions involving local officials, contractors and federal representatives, construction on the disputed land was halted temporarily.San Ygnacio has secured a temporary breather for now rather than a definitive victory. Whether its residents can once again persuade the government to respect their claims remains uncertain.
Article Summary: San Ygnacio, Texas is known for its historic sandstone houses, traditional architecture and long connection with the border region. In 1951, residents successfully persuaded the US government to spare their community from condemnation for a federal dam project. Nearly 75 years later, the town is once again resisting a major government development; this time a proposed border wall. Residents fear the loss of vegetation and changes to the riverfront could damage the habitat they have spent decades protecting.

Article Title: Florida put radioactive fertiliser waste beneath a private road; 4 test sections are being monitored for safety
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How will the Florida road project be monitored for safety

PC: AI Generated

Why is the material considered a radiation and health concern

How are stacks designed to limit exposure

Other uses of phosphogypsum under EPA rules

A waste material from fertiliser production is being tested for a new use in road construction in Florida. The material, known as phosphogypsum, is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid. It contains radium, which can decay into radioactive radon gas, so its use is regulated by the US Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA generally requires phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks that limit public exposure. However, some other uses can be approved when they provide at least as much protection.According to the US Environmental Protection Agency, one such project in New Wales, Florida, uses phosphogypsum in the road base beneath asphalt on private property. The agency determined that the project was as protective of human health as stacking the material.The EPA approved a phosphogypsum road construction project for Mosaic Fertilizer, LLC on December 23, 2024. The project is located on private property in New Wales, Florida. Phosphogypsum will be incorporated into the road base and covered with asphalt. The test road has four sections containing phosphogypsum in the road base, separated by four control sections without phosphogypsum.One upgradient monitoring well and two downgradient wells will be placed in each section. The property has controlled access, so members of the public are not expected to come into contact with the phosphogypsum in the test road. The EPA approved the request after determining that the proposed use was as protective of human health as placement of phosphogypsum in a stack.Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid, which is later used in fertilizer. The phosphate ore and the resulting phosphogypsum contain radium. Radium decays to form radon gas, which is radioactive and can cause cancer.The EPA says radon in outside air can enter structures and reach levels that pose a health hazard over time. Higher exposure to radon over prolonged periods can increase the risk of developing lung cancer. Phosphogypsum stacks also contain low-pH process water and heavy metals. Because radionuclides in phosphogypsum are a source of radon gas and direct gamma radiation, the EPA regulates phosphogypsum as a source category of radionuclides under the Clean Air Act.EPA regulations generally require phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks to limit public exposure from radon emissions. Owners and operators of inactive stacks must measure and report radon emissions and keep those emissions within regulatory limits. When phosphogypsum is placed on a stack, it is added as a liquid slurry.As the stack dewaters, the liquid effluent is captured, treated, tested, and discharged under the Clean Water Act. Newer stacks contain a liner to help prevent effluent from being released directly into soil and groundwater, while older stacks may not. When inactive, an engineered cover is typically placed over the phosphogypsum to prevent further water infiltration.EPA regulations allow phosphogypsum to be removed from stacks for outdoor agricultural purposes and indoor research and development under certain conditions and restrictions. Any other use requires prior EPA approval formally. The agency evaluates each proposed use case by case, considering how the phosphogypsum would be used, the amount involved, and possible health risks to workers and the public, including risks from handling and transportation. EPA can approve a proposed use only when it is at least as protective of public health as placing phosphogypsum in a stack.
Article Summary: Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid. It contains radium, which can decay into radioactive radon gas. The material is regulated by the US Environmental Protection Agency. Project in New Wales, Florida, uses the material in the road base beneath asphalt on private property.

Article Title: Indianapolis rebuilt a 10,000-foot airport runway using concrete that captures CO2 and stores it inside the pavement
Article Text:
In an industry first, Indy airport is using carbon capture technology on a full runway. Image Credit: Indianapolis Airport Authority/Engineering News-Record

How the 10,000-foot runway captures and stores CO2

The runway was rebuilt for long-term service

Concrete slabs are laid at Indianapolis International Airport. Image Credit: Woolpert/Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure

What happened to the old runway materials

Renewable energy added another layer of sustainability

The project earned the highest sustainability recognition

Indianapolis International Airport rebuilt its 10,000-foot-long Runway 5R-23L with concrete designed to capture and permanently store carbon dioxide inside the pavement. The $190 million reconstruction project introduced carbon-capture technology to an entire airport runway after receiving approval from the Federal Aviation Administration. The Indianapolis Airport Authority said the project was recognised with the Envision Platinum Award, the highest level awarded by the Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure. It combined the new concrete system with recycled construction materials, renewable energy and upgrades intended to improve the runway for decades.The central innovation is the use of CarbonCure technology in the concrete. According to Engineering News-Record, the system introduces recycled carbon dioxide into freshly mixed concrete during production. The gas then undergoes mineralisation, turning it into a solid mineral and permanently embedding it in the pavement.The Sustainable Infrastructure report explains that the project uses post-industrial CO2 in fresh concrete, where it converts into calcium carbonate. The process is intended to reduce the amount of carbon associated with the concrete while also improving its compressive strength without affecting other important properties of the material.The 22-inch top concrete layer of the reconstructed runway contains the captured carbon. Engineering News-Record reported that the amount of carbon expected to be stored was equivalent to the carbon associated with planting about 1.2 million trees.This was not simply a small demonstration section.
